What am I looking at?
The tolerance class/fit for this thread (how loose or tight it's allowed to be manufactured). For ISO Metric: 6g is the external (bolt/screw) class and 6H is the internal (nut/tapped hole) class - together the standard 'generous fit' pairing used for most commercial and industrial fasteners.
What am I looking at?
Which way the fastener tightens when turned clockwise, viewed from the head/driving end. Right-Hand (RH) is the standard used on the overwhelming majority of fasteners.
Right
Left (uncommon)
Right-Hand is the default and covers essentially all general-purpose fasteners. Left-Hand is an uncommon, special-purpose type - tightens counter-clockwise instead - used where the assembly needs to self-tighten under a rotating/reversing load or must not be interchangeable with a right-hand part. Typical examples: the left bicycle pedal, some gas-cylinder/propane valve connections (to prevent hooking up the wrong gas), and certain rotating machinery shafts.

Overall fastener length. Drives the Thread Coverage calculation (thread length vs. shank length); otherwise a visualization reference only.
Manufacturing
What am I looking at?
How the external thread is produced. Rolled/formed threads are cold-worked (stronger, smoother, more accurate); cut/ground/whirled/milled/chased threads remove material with a tool. Feeds the strength notes on the right.
Thread Rolling is the recommended baseline for external threads - the standard, most economical high-volume production method - unless your application specifically calls for a cut, ground, whirled, milled, or chased thread instead.
What am I looking at?
How the internal thread (tapped hole) is produced. Cut taps remove material; form/roll taps cold-form it (no chips, generally stronger). Feeds the strength notes on the right.
Thread cutting remains the most commonly used method for internal threads - it handles the widest range of materials and hole conditions (through or blind) without needing a dedicated form-tap setup. Reach for a form/roll tap when the application benefits from its cold-formed strength.
What am I looking at?
The fastener's base material. Used with Grade/Class below for the Thread Strength calculation - it does not change the thread geometry itself.
Used only for the Thread Strength calculation below. Options are filtered to the active thread standard's unit system (SAE J429 for inch, ISO 898-1 for metric).
Thread Locking Feature
What am I looking at?
An optional vibration-resistant coating applied over part of the thread (nylon patch or pre-applied adhesive patch). Adds a shaded band on the diagram and extra seating torque - purely a locking aid, not part of the base thread geometry.
°
Nylon Patch (IFI-124/524) is applied as a partial-circumference wedging stripe, not a full wrap - 120° TYP unless otherwise specified, with 90°-180° seen across manufacturers/sizes. The Pre-Applied Adhesive Patch (IFI-125/525) is always 360° full circumference by definition and has no Radial Angle control.
threads
Unless otherwise specified, X is 5 to 7 thread pitches of coating (TYP), per IFI-124/125 (inch) and IFI-524/525 (metric).
threads
Unless otherwise specified, Y is 1 to 3 thread pitches without coating (TYP) at each end, per IFI-124/125 (inch) and IFI-524/525 (metric) - left uncoated to allow easy starting and proper seating.

What is this tool?

Pick a thread standard and a size, and this tool draws you a clear picture of what that screw thread looks like - plus the measurements you'd need, like how wide it is, what drill bit makes a matching hole, and how far apart the "ridges" are. It covers the thread types you'll run into most often: metric, inch (UNC/UNF), pipe threads, ACME, and several others. Everything lives under three tabs at the top: the Visualizer (the drawing and calculator you're probably here for), the User Guide (this page), and Best Practices (a Thread Selector wizard, a standards library, pitch charts, and a plain-English design writeup).

How to use the Visualizer

  1. Choose your Fastener Type. Is it a bolt or screw, a nut, a tapped hole, a pipe fitting, or a self-tapping screw? This is the first choice on the left, and it decides what other options and pictures show up next. Not sure which standard even applies to your part? Hop over to Best Practices → Thread Selector first - it'll ask a few plain questions and drop you back here with the right one already picked.
  2. Pick a view. Right below Fastener Type, switch between Thread Profile (a picture of the thread shape) and Thread Coverage (a picture showing how much of the fastener is threaded).
  3. Pick the Standard and Size. Choose the thread standard (for example, "ISO Metric Coarse"), then a size from the list - just like reading it off a drawing or a box label. Got an unusual size? You can type the diameter and pitch in yourself instead. Small "i" buttons sit next to most fields - click one any time you want a plain-English reminder of what that field actually means.
  4. Set the Thread Class and Hand. Thread Class controls how loose or tight the fit is allowed to be (for metric, 6g/6H is the everyday default). Hand is almost always Right-Hand - Left-Hand is a special-purpose option for parts that need to tighten the "wrong" way.
  5. Enter the Length. This is the fastener's overall length - it drives the Thread Coverage picture (how much of that length ends up threaded) and shows on the drawing for reference.
  6. Pick how it's made. Under Manufacturing, Forming Method defaults to Thread Rolling for external threads - the most common, most economical method - switch to cut, ground, whirled, milled, or chased only if your application specifically calls for it. For an internal thread (nut/tapped hole), you'll instead see Tap Type. This changes the strength numbers slightly.
  7. Pick a Material, and a Grade if you know it. Material sets a default strength number; if you know the exact grade (like "SAE J429 Grade 8" or "ISO 898-1 Class 8.8"), the Grade/Class dropdown swaps in the real certified number instead of a generic average.
  8. Turn on a Locking Feature, if you need one. For a regular bolt or screw, you can add a nylon patch or adhesive patch to keep it from vibrating loose, and see roughly where it sits and how much extra torque it adds. A few extra fields (Radial Angle, Axial Length, Lead-in Clearance) appear once you pick one - the defaults shown are the typical values, so you can usually leave them as-is.
  9. Fill in the Mating Material, if the Thread Strength panel is showing. This is whatever the fastener threads into (a nut, or the tapped hole itself) - it feeds the Thread Strength (Tensile & Stripping) numbers on the right, explained below.
  10. Copy your callout. On the right, you'll find a ready-made thread callout (like "M8 x 1.25 - 6g") you can paste straight into an email, drawing, or part number - just click the small copy icon next to it.
  11. Print, if you need a paper or PDF copy. The Print button in the top-right corner of the page builds a clean, standalone reference sheet (SBS letterhead, no on-screen buttons or menus) with the current spec, diagram, and notes - ready to print or save as a PDF from your browser's print dialog.

Reading the picture

The main picture is a side-on "slice" through the fastener, so you can see the thread shape clearly. Hover over any labeled part - Crest, Root, Flank, Pitch - for a plain-English explanation. Quick cheat sheet:

  • Crest - the top of a ridge.
  • Root - the bottom of the groove between two ridges.
  • Flank - the sloped side connecting a crest to a root.
  • Pitch - the distance from one thread to the next.

The small "V" marker near the top-left is the Thread Angle - the actual angle between the two sides of a ridge, always matching the real spec value for whichever standard you've picked. The colored lines running along the drawing are the Major, Minor, and Pitch diameters - three different "widths" of the thread, each measured at a different point. One quirk: for an internal thread (like inside a nut), Major and Minor swap places compared to a regular bolt. Click anywhere on the drawing for a bigger, fully labeled close-up.

Understanding the Calculated Values panel

On the right, results are grouped into a few cards:

  • Diameters and Thread Geometry - the raw dimensions for the size and standard you've picked (major/minor/pitch diameter, tap drill size, clearance hole, and so on), plus your selected Size, Pitch, and Thread Class right at the top of the Diameters card. For ISO Metric Coarse/Fine threads, two classes now show a real max/min tolerance band instead of a single nominal number: external threads at class 6g show it on Major and Pitch Diameter (e.g. "3.978 - 3.838 mm", an approximate ISO 965-1 formula calculation), and internal threads (hex nut, tapped hole) at class 6H show it on Major, Pitch, and Minor Diameter instead - for the 13 ISO Metric Coarse sizes (M1.6 through M24), the 6H numbers come straight from the published ASME B1.13M Table 12 (Major Diameter is labelled "reference only", matching that table's own heading, since it isn't a functionally toleranced dimension for a nut or tapped hole); ISO Metric Fine sizes aren't in that table, so they fall back to the same kind of formula approximation used for 6g, flagged as lower-confidence in its own note. Every other standard/class combination still shows the single nominal value only.
  • Strength and Fit - a quick-reference summary tied to the Thread Class you selected.
  • Thread Strength (Tensile & Stripping) - only appears once you've filled in a Material and Mating Material. It answers a real design question: if this joint were pulled apart, which would give out first - the bolt snapping in tension, or the threads themselves stripping? The header shows the formula it uses, F = Su × A, and just underneath it, in plain terms: F is the failure load (how much force it takes to break, in pounds-force or newtons), Su is the material's ultimate tensile strength (how much stress it can take before failing, in psi or MPa), and A is the relevant area that force is spread across - the bolt's own cross-section for a straight break, or the thread's contact area for stripping. Good design aims for the bolt to break before the threads strip, since a stripped joint can fail with no visible warning - the note box below the table calls out which failure mode is the weaker one for your current inputs.

Screw Thread Design reference

Allowance/tolerance/fit, UNR and UNJ (rounded-root) thread variants, cut vs. rolled threads (with a side-by-side photo comparison), thread strength/stripping basics, Go/No-Go gauging (also with a photo), fine-vs-coarse trade-offs, and manufacturing method guidance (including why Thread Rolling is this tool's recommended default for external threads) have all been consolidated in one place: the Screw Thread Design tab under Best Practices. Head there for the full writeup - it also covers common selection mistakes, minimum thread engagement rules of thumb by material, and the pre-callout validation checks worth running before you commit a thread callout to a drawing or part number.

Thread Coverage view

Switch to this view (next to Thread Profile) to answer a simple question: for this length of fastener, is it threaded all the way to the head, or just partway? Pick the specific bolt/screw standard whose published thread-length rule you want to use (it doesn't have to match your Thread Profile standard), and the picture shows the threaded portion versus the unthreaded shank, based on that standard's own formula.

A few extras you might see

Locking Feature picture - only shows up for a regular bolt or screw (not pipe fittings, power-transmission screws, or self-tapping screws), since that's what nylon/adhesive patches are actually made for. Turning it on adds a shaded band on the main drawing plus a second, same-size picture looking straight down the tip, showing how far around the fastener the coating wraps.

Point Style panel - for self-tapping screws, shows a picture and short description of that type's real-world tip shape (pointed, blunt, and so on).

Shank shape for Taptite II / Plastite 48-2 - these two screw types have a three-lobed shank instead of a round one, which is what lets them form their own mating thread. Selecting either one opens a second, same-size picture comparing that shape to a standard round hole - and their main thread picture shows a rounded crest and sharp root instead of the usual flat top, since that's how these threads are actually formed.

Grade / Class selector - lets you pick a specific material grade (like "Grade 8") instead of a generic average, for a more accurate strength number. Not sure? Leaving it on "Generic" gives a reasonable ballpark. The same idea applies to Mating Grade / Class for whatever the fastener threads into.

Plastic Boss Design Reference - if a self-tapping screw is driving into a molded plastic boss, this gives you a starting-point size for the pilot hole, boss, and engagement depth, scaled to the screw. It's a starting point, not a substitute for your plastic supplier's own guidance.

The "i" info buttons - next to most field labels, these open a short plain-English explanation of that field without leaving the page. Handy if you just want a quick refresher instead of digging through this guide.

The Best Practices tab, at a glance

Four sub-tabs live under Best Practices, each covering a different kind of reference:

  • Thread Selector - a short, guided Q&A that helps you land on the right thread standard when you're not sure where to start, then jumps you straight into the Visualizer with it already chosen.
  • Standards Reference - a table of every standard this tool implements or cites, each with its title, what it's used for, and (for the ones on file) a View Standard button linking to the actual document. Standards without a link on file are marked Coming Soon.
  • Thread Pitch Charts - every standard's full size/pitch table in one printable reference, grouped by thread family, with checkboxes to build your own custom printout.
  • Screw Thread Design - the plain-language design writeup described above.

A quick word of caution

This tool is built to make everyday thread lookups fast and easy, using standard published formulas. It's great for getting familiar numbers, checking your own math, or explaining a thread to someone else. It isn't a substitute for the official governing standard or your engineering drawing, and it shouldn't be the final word on production tolerances or quality sign-off. For anything going into manufacturing or a customer commitment, always double-check the real standard and your drawing requirements first. Specialty Bolt and Screw, Inc. isn't liable for decisions made using this tool's output.

Screw Thread Design

  • A plain-language walkthrough of how and why threads are designed the way they are - the small gap built into every thread on purpose, the difference between rounded and sharp thread roots, how threads are actually made, and what makes a threaded joint strong (or not).
  • Plus practical tips for getting accurate, consistent results out of this tool and the thread callouts it helps you produce.

Why Threads Aren't Cut "Perfectly" On Purpose

  • Every real thread is made a little looser than its "ideal" size - on purpose. That built-in gap is called the allowance, and it guarantees there's always a little room to assemble the parts, even after accounting for normal manufacturing variation. It's usually built into the external thread (the bolt or screw).
  • Tolerance is a related but different idea: it's just how much a measurement is allowed to vary - the gap between the biggest and smallest size still considered acceptable.
  • Allowance and tolerance together decide the thread's fit - how loose or snug it feels going together. A clearance fit spins on freely; an interference fit is intentionally tight and needs a tool to run the nut down at first.
  • For inch threads, that fit is labeled with a class - 1A/1B, 2A/2B, or 3A/3B ("A" is for external threads like bolts, "B" is for internal threads like nuts). All three are still clearance fits (they always go together without forcing), but the higher the number, the snugger and more precise the fit:
  • 1A/1B - very loose and quick to assemble. Not common outside threaded rod or basic machine screws.
  • 2A/2B - the everyday, general-purpose choice. About 90% of commercial and industrial fasteners use this one.
  • 3A/3B - a snug, no-slack fit for parts where safety really matters. Socket-head fasteners typically use this class.
  • Metric threads use a similar idea with different labels - 6g (external) paired with 6H (internal) is the everyday metric pairing, playing the same role 2A/2B plays for inch threads.
  • One more term worth knowing: how far the bolt and nut's threads actually overlap once assembled is called the length of thread engagement - basically, how much thread is really "in contact." It's one of the biggest levers a designer has for making a joint stronger (more on exactly how much it helps, and where it stops helping, further down).

Rounded vs. Sharp Thread Roots (UNR and UNJ)

  • The bottom of a thread groove (the "root") can be cut sharp or left slightly rounded. A rounded root resists cracking and fatigue better than a sharp one, so two common Unified thread variants build the rounding in on purpose:
  • UNR - a modest, required rounding at the root. This is what you get automatically from thread rolling (see below), which is why almost every rolled fastener made today is technically a UNR thread - and it comes with a real fatigue-life benefit at no extra cost.
  • UNJ - a noticeably bigger root radius, used mainly in aerospace. Because the rounding is larger, a UNJ bolt needs its own matching UNJ nut - it isn't guaranteed to thread into a standard nut.

How Threads Are Made, and What Actually Makes a Joint Strong

  • There are two ways to cut a thread: cutting it away with a die or lathe (which slices through the material's internal grain structure), or rolling it - squeezing a smooth blank between grooved dies so the material flows into shape, a bit like squeezing a balloon between your fingers.
  • Rolled threads generally come out more accurate, smoother, and stronger - especially for resisting fatigue and shear. Cutting is simpler and cheaper to tool up for, and it's still the usual way internal threads (tapped holes) get made.
  • That's why this tool defaults to Thread Rolling for external (bolt/screw) threads - it's the standard, most cost-effective choice for volume production. Other methods (grinding, whirling, milling) have their place too, but usually only for special cases like hardened precision threads or long, slender lead screws.
  • Now, what actually breaks first in an overloaded threaded joint? A bolt pulled in straight tension eventually snaps - that's one failure mode. But there's a second, sneakier one: thread stripping, where the threads themselves shear off instead of the bolt breaking. Whichever material (the bolt or the nut/tapped hole) is weaker is the one that strips.
  • Good design aims for the bolt to be the "fuse" - it should snap in an obvious way before the threads quietly strip, since a stripped joint can fail without any visible warning. The simple rule: pick a nut whose rated strength (called proof stress) is at least as high as the bolt's own tensile strength. If the nut is the weak link, stripping - not a clean bolt break - becomes the likely way the joint fails.
Cut thread (left) vs. rolled thread (right) - rolling forms the pitch diameter by displacing material rather than cutting it away.

Fine Threads or Coarse Threads?

  • For the same size fastener, you can usually choose a coarser thread (UNC / ISO Metric Coarse) or a finer one (UNF / ISO Metric Fine) - and neither is simply "better." It's a genuine trade-off both ways. The Pitch badge next to the diagram, and the Thread Pitch Charts in this tool, make it easy to see the exact numbers for any size you're comparing.
Why choose a fine thread
  • Stronger in straight tension, since more material remains at the same overall size.
  • Handles twisting and side-load forces a bit better too.
  • Easier to tap into thin-walled parts, where a coarse thread's deeper groove leaves too little material to grip.
  • Finer adjustment - useful for parts that need to be positioned precisely.
Why choose a coarse thread
  • Better resistance to stripping for the same length of engagement.
  • Handles repeated stress (fatigue) better.
  • Much less likely to cross-thread (start crooked) during assembly.
  • Faster to assemble and disassemble, and works better in brittle materials like cast iron.
  • Leaves more room for thick platings or coatings.
  • Both sides have good arguments - but as more assembly has become automated, the industry has quietly leaned more toward coarse threads over time, mainly because they're more forgiving to assemble by machine.

Go/No-Go Gauges: How a Thread Gets "Passed" or "Failed"

  • A Go/No-Go gauge is a simple pass/fail check - a threaded ring (for checking bolts) or a threaded plug (for checking nuts/holes) - used to confirm a real, manufactured thread actually falls inside its allowed size range, not just that it "looks about right."
  • The Go gauge represents the largest acceptable size and has to thread on smoothly. If it won't go, the part's thread is too big (for a bolt) or too small (for a hole) and it fails inspection.
  • The No-Go gauge represents the smallest acceptable size and should barely start, then stop - if it keeps threading past a turn or two, the part was cut too far and also fails.
  • Using both together catches both problems: too big and too small. Only a thread that's genuinely within the allowed size range passes both checks.
  • One practical detail: plated parts (like standard zinc-plated bolts) are often gauged with a slightly tighter Go gauge before plating, since the plating itself adds a small amount of thickness back on. Minor cosmetic damage - small dents, scrapes, or plating buildup - usually isn't cause for rejection unless it actually affects how the part functions.
A combination Go/No-Go gauge - the Go end checks against Maximum Material Condition (MMC), the No-Go end checks against Least Material Condition (LMC).

Why the First Few Threads Do Most of the Work

  • Here's a counterintuitive fact: when a bolt and nut are under load, the engaged threads don't share the load evenly. The very first thread to engage carries the biggest share by far - often around a third of the entire load by itself - with each thread behind it carrying a bit less.
  • This happens because standard nut material is deliberately made a little softer than the bolt, so the first thread can yield slightly and pass some of the load along instead of taking it all alone. Use a nut that's harder than intended, and you lose that safety margin - which can actually promote fatigue or loosening instead of helping.
  • This is also why making a joint's engagement longer and longer doesn't keep adding strength forever. Once that hardest-working first thread reaches its limit, it gives way and hands the load to the next one in line, and the benefit of extra length tapers off quickly after that.
  • As a rule of thumb: for ordinary steel fasteners, engagement much beyond about one bolt diameter in length stops adding meaningful strength. Softer materials like aluminum need a bit more - roughly 1.5× the diameter - to reach a similar safety margin.
  • The practical takeaway for picking a nut: choose one whose rated strength (proof stress) is at least as high as the bolt's own tensile strength, and make sure its spec is meant to pair with the bolt's spec (for example, matching ASTM or SAE standards). Undersize the nut, and stripping - not a clean bolt break - becomes the likely failure.

Minimum Thread Engagement by Material (Rule of Thumb)

  • "Thread engagement" gets used two different ways, so it's worth being clear on which one is meant: length of engagement is a literal measurement - how much threaded length ends up inside the nut once everything is seated (a 1 inch bolt threaded into a 0.5 inch nut has 0.5 inch of engagement). Percentage of engagement is a different idea - it's about how well the bolt's and nut's thread heights actually overlap, not how long the engagement is.
  • The Thread Strength calculation elsewhere in this tool works out the exact length of engagement needed, based on your specific materials. The quick rule-of-thumb numbers below (from Associated Fastening Products, Inc.'s "What is Thread Engagement?" reference) are a faster gut-check for the same question - just a simple multiple of the bolt's diameter, no calculation needed.
Quick rule of thumb, by the material being threaded into
  • Aluminum - engage at least 2.0 to 2.5× the bolt's diameter.
  • Brass or cast iron - engage at least 1.5 to 2.0× the bolt's diameter.
  • Steel - engage at least 1.0 to 1.5× the bolt's diameter.
For a steel bolt specifically, by what it's threading into
  • Into steel - 1.0× the bolt's diameter. Typical for everyday industrial and structural assemblies.
  • Into aluminum or brass - 1.5× the bolt's diameter. Common in engine blocks, electronics housings, and lightweight frames.
  • Into cast iron - 1.25 to 1.5× the bolt's diameter. Common in heavy machinery and automotive parts.
  • Into plastic or composite - 2.0× the bolt's diameter or more. Common in consumer products and chemical equipment.
  • Think of these as a fast sanity check, not a replacement for the full calculation above (or a certified engineering value) on anything safety-critical. Notice they point the same direction as the calculation: softer, weaker materials simply need more engagement length to reach the bolt's full strength.

Common Mistakes Worth Double-Checking

Easy to get wrong
  • Mixing up coarse and fine threads - the same nominal size has a different pitch in each series, so a 1/4-20 (coarse) tap will not fit a 1/4-28 (fine) hole, even though both say "1/4."
  • Assuming a metric and an inch thread that "look about the same size" are interchangeable - M6x1.0 and 1/4-20 are close in diameter but are not the same thread. Always match the actual standard, not just the approximate size.
  • Choosing a fit class without checking what it mates with - two different classes can still technically screw together, so double-check the resulting fit is actually what the application needs (see Double-Checks Before You Finalize a Callout below).
  • Treating UNJ threads as a drop-in replacement for standard threads - the bigger root radius means a UNJ bolt isn't guaranteed to fit a standard nut, and calling out UNJ also implies the tighter aerospace-grade tolerance, not just a "premium" version of a regular thread.
  • Forgetting to call out Left-Hand when it's actually needed - a part ordered without that note defaults to ordinary Right-Hand, and it simply will not thread onto a left-hand mating part.
  • Picking a nut without checking its strength against the bolt - see "Why the First Few Threads Do Most of the Work" above; an undersized nut invites a quiet thread-stripping failure instead of an obvious bolt break.
  • Treating a self-tapping screw's size like a regular machine screw size - pilot hole, point style, and material thickness all interact for self-tapping screws; a combination that works great in sheet metal may not work at all in molded plastic (see the Plastic Boss Design Reference for that case).

Double-Checks Before You Finalize a Callout

A quick checklist before it goes on a drawing or part number
  • Does the Thread Class match the actual part - external (bolt) vs. internal (nut)? This tool's dropdown only shows valid options for what you've selected, so if there's just one choice, that's the right one.
  • Did the Major Diameter and Pitch actually come from picking a real size, and not get left over from a different standard you looked at earlier? (These fields are locked to the size dropdown specifically to prevent that mix-up.)
  • Have you cross-checked the tap drill and clearance hole sizes shown here against your shop's own reference chart before cutting metal? Treat this tool's numbers as a helpful reference, not the final word.
  • Is Hand (Right- or Left-Hand) actually correct for the application, and is it clearly written on the drawing or part number if Left-Hand is needed?
  • For self-tapping screws, do the point style and pilot hole actually suit the real material and thickness being driven into - not just the nominal screw size?
  • If a Thread Locking Feature (like a nylon or adhesive patch) is called out, does it match what the application actually needs? See the User Guide and Standards Reference for the specific IFI numbers.

A Simple Workflow to Follow

A practical order of operations
  1. Not sure which standard applies? Start in Thread Selector - answer a few questions and it drops you into the Visualizer with the right standard already chosen.
  2. In the Visualizer, confirm the Fastener Category, Nominal Size, Thread Class, and Hand, then look over the diagram and the Engineering Callout box.
  3. Run through the Double-Checks above against the actual drawing, purchase order, or part number before it's finalized.
  4. For anything going into production or out to a customer, confirm it against the official governing standard - this tool is a fast, helpful reference, not the final authority (see the User Guide for more on that).

A Few More Things Worth Knowing

Worth remembering while you work
  • The thread diagram is drawn for clarity, not to exact scale, on every standard (see the User Guide's "Reading the picture" section). The Detail View's triangle overlay is a general 60° reference, not a live recalculation for non-60° thread shapes like ACME, Buttress, Whitworth, or Square - the caption underneath tells you which case you're looking at.
  • Any links you save in the Standards Reference table are stored only in this browser, on this computer - they won't follow the file if you open it somewhere else, so you'd need to re-add them.
  • Torn between two similar standards - say, Coarse vs. Fine, metric or inch? The User Guide's Fine-vs-Coarse comparison table walks through the practical trade-offs in plain terms.
